Building Web Pages with React

Chapter Overview

» React is a JavaScript library for building interfaces

» React uses Next.js to provide backend capabilities

» Components are reusable building blocks in React

React is a JavaScript library that is primarily focused on building user interfaces in JavaScript. While similar in spirit to our reusable HTML component design pattern we’ve explored in previous chapters, React brings the concept of creating reusable components to the forefront with its use of the innovative JavaScript XML (JSX) syntax. JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write code that looks like HTML right inside JavaScript.

React was written by Jordan Walke at Facebook. It was released to the public in May 2013 (June 2, 2013 on GitHub) and was used internally within Facebook and then later in the interface revamp of Instagram. Since then, it has become a wildly popular JavaScript framework. Even if you don’t plan on using React (but at some point you probably will), you’ll need to be familiar with it so that you can maintain and modify existing code.

While we won’t rebuild our framework in React, it’s still worth exploring. The goal here isn’t to cover React fully, but rather to offer a quick tour of its capabilities and some hands-on exercises that will help you become familiar with the framework. React is the front half of the full-stack framework; however, using the same language to build the frontend as well as the backend gives you a seamless development experience.

Creating a New React Site

React has a bit of a different workflow than we’ve been using through most of this book, and that’s largely due to the most common way to run a React website—through Next.js. The Next.js portion of this stack provides the backend capabilities, offering tight integration with React.

React websites should live in a separate folder, so, in Visual Studio Code, open your Source folder ( File > Open Folder… > Select Folder ) and create a new folder within it called coffee-shop-react . To create this new folder, mouse up to the top of the Explorer pane in VS Code and a series of icons should appear. Click the Folder icon with the plus ( figure 35 ).

Once you’ve created the coffee-shop-react folder, right click on it and click Open in Integrated Terminal . This will open a terminal/console window pane in Visual Studio Code. In this window, type (at the -> prompt) 

npx create-next-app@latest .

…and press ENTER.

The dot at the end of the command tells Node.js to create the React site within the coffee-shop-react folder. If you don’t specify it, a folder within coffee-shop-react called coffee-shop-react will be created, which is not what we want. Please don’t forget the dot!

You may receive a notice about the necessity of installing packages. If so, simply press ENTER to confirm. You’ll be asked some questions. Here are the answers to provide, pressing ENTER after each to confirm.

» What is your project name? coffee-shop-react

» Would you like to use TypeScript? No (toggle answer with arrow keys)

» Would you like to use ESLint? Yes

» Would you like to use Tailwind CSS? Yes

» Would you like to use a src directory? No

» Use App Router? Yes

» Would you like to customize the default import alias? No

Versions of React in the future might ask different questions. If you’re not sure of the answer, the default is probably fine.

Once this new project wizard process completes, you’ll have files ready to go for your React project ( figure 36 ).

Understanding the React Application Structure

Let’s walk through the structure that was just created so we can understand the purpose and function of the files and folders within a typical React application.

We’ll start with the files in the root of the folder first, then work through the folders. We’ll cover many of these in more depth as we progress through the chapter ( table 10 ):

File / Folder

Purpose

.eslintrc.json

Configuration file for ESLint, which is an analysis tool that helps find bugs and design issues within JavaScript.

.gitignore

A file created to instruct Git, the source code version control system, which files should not be included in a repository and should remain only on your computer.

next.config.js

The configuration file for the Next.js web framework.

package-lock.json

A file automatically generated by npm that sets versions of dependencies to ensure the package will install and run correctly on another computer.

package.json

A configuration file that details the dependencies for the project.

postcss.config.js

Configuration file for PostCSS, which facilitates the transformation of styles with various JavaScript plugins, preventing conflicts.

README.md

A Markdown file that contains information about the project. This is especially helpful for other developers.

tailwind.config.js

The Tailwind CSS configuration file, a CSS framework that makes it easy to quickly add helpful styles to your HTML.

app

The folder containing the React JavaScript files.

node_modules

The dependency files for the project are stored within this folder.

public

This folder contains files that will be served directly to the browser rather than be processed as part of the React app.

For more information on Markdown, please see www.markdownguide.org

Now let’s look inside the app folder. This is where the bulk of the React website’s code resides. You’ll see at least four files here by default ( table 11 ):

File / Folder

Purpose

favicon.ico

The icon displayed for the site in bookmarks. You can replace this with your website’s logo in ico format.

globals.css

This CSS file is meant to house CSS styles that will apply to your entire React site. Tailwind CSS will also include some boilerplate code here to import its styles and utilities.

layout.js

JavaScript code here generally applies to the entire site, providing navigation elements, header/footer components, and other site-wide features.

page.js

The primary landing page of the site.

The page.js file in the app folder exports the Home component, which is part of what defines what appears on the landing page (i.e., the home page) of the site.

There are two folders that don’t appear in the default file structure, but are nevertheless quite important: the pages and components folders.

In the pages folder, you can place files, like about.js , and they will provide the code necessary for a page with the URL /about . As you might expect, pages/contact.js would serve /contact .

In the components folder, components are defined that can be used for the React website.

Building Components

Components are at the heart of React. Just like in our framework, React encourages component reuse by making it simple to define reusable bits of code that make up your interface.

Let’s take a look at a simple component. Don’t type this code quite yet. I want to introduce the concept of components first before we actually start writing React code. 

import React from "react"

function Greeting() {
   return (
      <div>
         <p>Hello, World!</p>
      </div>
   )
}

The first thing that might stick out to you about this code is that the name of the function, Greeting , starts with an uppercase letter. In React, component names begin with a capital letter. Also, the HTML within the function should be in all lowercase, although this is the standard we’ve already been following in this book.

What’s unique here is that this function returns HTML—not by writing to the document or using innerHTML-type functionality, but by embedding the HTML directly into the JavaScript code. This is JSX, which contains HTML, but also has other functionality that makes a component far more useful than simply being able to regurgitate HTML. 

import React from "react"

function Greeting(props) {
   return (
      <div>
         <p>Hello, {props.firstName}!</p>
      </div>
   )
}

In this version of the Greeting component, we accept an argument, props , and then use the firstName property of that object to pass to the component the first name we want to greet.

Now that we’ve built this component, to use it, we simply use it in our HTML, like this: 

<Greeting />

We just constructed something akin to a new HTML element within React! Pretty neat, huh? If we want to pass a value to it, we simply use this syntax: 

<Greeting firstName="Robert" />

That was a bit of a simplification. If you’d like to see a more detailed component, check out the app/page.js file to see the Home component that is designed for you by default. It contains a fair bit of code, so we’ll save paper and not print it here, but this serves as a typical example.

You don’t have to use function to define a component. In the next example, you’ll notice that rather than use function to start a component definition, I use const . Both methods are acceptable. It generally comes down to personal preference, with one small distinction: If you use function , you can use components anywhere without having to define them first. If you use const , you must define the components first. Put your components within JavaScript files in the components folder, then import them at the top of files that use them, so this won’t be an issue.

I recommend choosing either the const or function method and sticking with it, at least within the same project—unless there’s a strong need to deviate from the convention you establish. 

import React from "react"

const AlertButton = ({ alertMessage }) => {
   const handleClick = () => {
      alert(alertMessage)
   }

   return (
      <button onClick={handleClick}>
         Click Me
      </button>
   )
}

const Greeting = () => {
   return (
      <div>
         <AlertButton alertMessage="Hello, World!" />
      </div>
   )
}

You have probably noticed we’re doing more than simply introducing a new convention ( const )—we’re nesting components and binding events to them! We’ll tackle each separately.

First, let’s address the concept of nesting components. This is an incredibly useful feature that lets you build even smaller, yet highly functional and flexible, components. I recommend nesting components as much as practical, because the smaller and more self-contained the building block you build, the more you can reuse it. For example, you can use this AlertButton component anytime you need this kind of functionality. By passing the message as a property, you give it the ability to adapt to a wide range of situations.

Second, let’s discuss binding events. JavaScript, at its heart, is event-driven, so binding functionality to events that happen is second nature to the language. React extends this functionality by letting us encapsulate the event within the component, creating a reusable object that can handle its own actions. The handleClick function, as its name suggests, handles the activity upon the click of the button, and this is bound to the button by passing it to the onClick event, with {handleClick} in curly braces.

Using Components in Other Files

When you define a component, you’ll want to save it in the components folder. I say “want to” because you don’t strictly have to, but this is the convention with React, and it’s best to stick with that convention. The filename should be capitalized just like the name of the component.

For example, if we defined a Greeting component… 

const Greeting = () => {
   return (
      <div>
         <p>Hello, World!</p>
      </div>
   )
}
export default Greeting

…we would name it Greeting.js and place it in the components folder. Note that I’ve added the export default Greeting line at the end. This tells JavaScript to make this object available to other files that include it.

To use the Greeting component, we’d preface the file that used it with… 

import Greeting from "../components/Greeting.js"

The two dots before /components tell JavaScript to go up one directory (to the root of the React app), then go into the components folder to look for the file Greeting.js . This assumes that the file using the component (i.e., the file with the import ) would be in another folder, like pages —which is common practice anyway within a React app.

Designing in React

As you’ve seen by now, the React paradigm is a bit different from standard JavaScript. We’ve previously discussed reusable components, but thinking in components is vital to designing React websites and applications. To illustrate this point quite literally, let’s look at a typical (and simple) page layout ( figure 37 ):

Just like the DOM structure resembles trees and their branches in describing the hierarchy of a web page, the same thoughtful nesting of components can save us time and make our design incredibly efficient. If I were going to determine the component structure of the sample web page layout in figure 38 , I would arrange it in the following manner:

» Header

» Logo

» Primary Navigation

» Social Links

» Content

» Full-width Section

» Content Teasers

» Teaser 1

» Teaser 2

» Teaser 3

» Footer

» Social Links

Now let’s create the same structure with components. Since HTML and CSS aren’t our focus, we’ll skip styling and a lot of the HTML that would be needed to actually give these items a great visual appeal. 

import Image from "next/image"

const Logo = () => (
   <Image src="logo.png" alt="Our Logo" />
)

const PrimaryNavigation = ({ links }) => (
   <div>
      {links.map((link, index) => (
         <a href={link.page}>{link.name}</a>
      ))}
   </div>
)

const SocialLinks = ({ socialAccounts }) => (
   <div>
      {socialAccounts.map((account, index) => (
         <a href={account.link}>{account.site}</a>
      ))}
   </div>
)

const FullWidthSlider = ({ slides }) => (
   <div>
      {slides.map((slide, index) => (
         <a href={slide.link}><img src={slide.image} alt={`Slide ${index}`} /></a>
      ))}
   </div>
)

const Teaser = ({ thumbnail, text }) => (
   <div>
      <img src={thumbnail} alt="thumbnail" />
      <div>
         {text}
      </div>
   </div>
)

const Header = ({ links, socialAccounts }) => (
   <div>
      <Logo />
      <PrimaryNavigation links={links} />
      <SocialLinks socialAccounts={socialAccounts} />
   </div>
)

const Content = ({ slides, teaserThumbnails, teaserTexts }) => (
   <div>
      <FullWidthSlider slides={slides} />
      <Teaser
         thumbnail={teaserThumbnails[0]}
         text={teaserTexts[0]}
      />
   </div>
)

const Footer = ({ socialAccounts }) => (
   <SocialLinks socialAccounts={socialAccounts} />
)

Let’s walk through some important aspects of this code.

First, you may notice that I define the components in the general order of least complex to most complex. This lets us nest components more easily. For example, the Header uses the SocialLinks component, but this could also exist anywhere else in the page, so it makes sense to define this ahead of time.

Even though the Logo component is simple and only used once on this page, defining this standalone item gives us expandability in the future. Let’s say we change the logo from a portable network graphic file (PNG file) to a scalable vector graphic file (SVG file). Doing so would be easier with this Logo component. It would also let us use the logo in multiple places on the page more easily. Perhaps in the future we could even accept a property that lets us use various versions to accommodate dark mode, black and white, and the like.

Second, we are using the map method to iterate over arrays passed to the components. We covered the map method in chapter 14 , but in essence, we’re making use of the temporary variables assigned from the values in the array in each pass. This generates a list of links (in the case of PrimaryNavigation and SocialLinks ) and a list of links with images (in the case of FullWidthSlider ). The HTML we generate obviously needs more styling, but the concepts work well.

Let’s look at an example for handling products. Imagine a data structure of coffee products: 

const inventory = [
   { productName: "Coffee", price: "3.95", inStock: true },
   { category: "Espresso", price: "4.49", inStock: true },
   { category: "Cappuccino", price: "4.95", inStock: false }
]

A component could iterate through the inventory like this:

const InventoryList = ({ inventory }) => {
   return (
      <div>
         {inventory.map((item, index) => (
            <div id={index}>
               <h2>{item.productName}</h2>
               <p>Price: ${item.price}</p>
               <p>In Stock: {item.inStock ? 'Yes' : 'No'}</p>
            </div>))}
      </div>
   )
}

The inventory data JSON can come from a remote server—it need not necessarily be included directly in your React website. And the data supplied by the remote server can come from an SQL server, like MySQL, Microsoft SQL, or even SQLite.

Managing Your Code with Git

Chapter Overview

» Source code management makes collaboration easier

» Git is a popular source code management system

» GitHub is a popular Git repository hosting service

Up until now, our programs have just been text documents on our machine. Each change we made overwrites the existing content. This might not seem like an issue, until we alter a working program at 11 p.m. and accidentally break something, causing a website to crash with no easy means of recovery. This may or may not be the voice of experience. But it is entirely preventable.

With version tracking, we have a log of all our code changes. We also get a backup if we sync with a remote location or provider. Source code management is the process of tracking changes in code and synchronizing them for purposes of collaboration.

Before I learned about source code management, anytime I worked on a program with others, we would work out a sometimes convoluted scheme to only work on files others weren’t editing. That strategy can be effective, but often results in lots of exchanged messages asking who’s working on what file. And the inevitable collision that can occur creates plenty of headaches for everyone. This approach has numerous flaws and didn’t carry over well to modern development methodologies.

In this chapter, we’ll learn about the Git source code management system, released to the public in 2005 by Linus Torvalds. If that name sounds familiar, it’s because Linus also started the Linux kernel, used in countless devices and in most of the world’s servers today. Since the release of Git, the software has enjoyed massive success, in part due to its fantastic branching support and the ease of merging those branches.

Branching is the process of copying code to a new, separate version in a software project. Unique branches move forward with new versions in parallel, and merging brings those versions back together, integrating the changes into a unified copy. Much like a road can add lanes in more populated or traffic-prone areas, then merge back into fewer lanes when it reaches the countryside.

Software code is stored in Git repositories. A repository is the container that stores source code. On a computer, a Git repository is just a folder of code (and possibly subfolders) with a .git folder in the main folder. This .git folder acts like a journal that contains the history of code changes. A Git repository can be pushed to a remote copy for collaboration and backup purposes.

GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are popular Git repository hosting companies, but anyone can host a repository themselves, because Git is open source. In this chapter, we’ll focus on local repositories and syncing with GitHub; however, the techniques we explore here should be compatible with other Git hosting.

Installing Git

Before you can use Git, you will need to install it on your computer. Visit https://git-scm.com/ and click the download button to see instructions for your platform. Windows users will need to download the installer and run it. On macOS, you can install Homebrew (see https://brew.sh/ ) to install Git. Once you’ve installed Homebrew, run brew install git to install Git.

Debian/Ubuntu/Linux Mint users need to run apt install git . Linux Arch-based distributions such as Arch and Manjaro need to run pacman -S git . Red Hat-based distributions would run yum install git .

Once Git is installed, you should be able to open a terminal or console and run… 

git version

…and you’ll see the version of Git installed. If you see a message like “command not found,” Git isn’t installed properly, so check the download/install instructions for your platform and try again.

Windows and macOS users can also install GitHub Desktop from https://desktop.github.com/ . GitHub Desktop is a wonderful Git management tool that makes it easy to graphically manage Git repositories. Though I find it very useful and have recommended it to others, I am not covering it in this chapter because it isn’t available for all platforms. You may not have it on the system you’re on (or on a remote system you’ve connected to), so it’s good to know how to use Git without it.

That said, if you’re running Windows or macOS and prefer a graphical solution, it might be a good fit for you.

Visual Studio Code also has Git support, but in the interest of providing you the most compatible and widespread coverage of knowledge, in this chapter we will focus on the command-line version of Git.

Forking and Cloning the ClydeBank Coffee Shop Website

The first step in using existing code on GitHub is to fork it to our own account. Forking a repository copies it to our account and lets us work with the code, including making changes of our own, without interfering with the original copy. We can later request the changes we made be integrated into the original project with a pull request . A pull request asks the maintainer(s) of the original project for permission to merge our changes into the main project.

Before you can fork the project, you’ll need to make a free account on GitHub. Navigate to https://github.com/ and create an account, then navigate to https://github.com/clydebankmedia/JavaScript-QuickStartGuide and click the fork button at the top right of the screen. This puts a copy of the repository in your account. Then you can clone , or download, the repository to your computer, where you’ll be able to access and edit the files.

When you click on the green <> Code icon ( figure 38 ) above the code in GitHub, you’ll see the commands for cloning the repository. The simplest variant is HTTPS, but if you know how to use SSH keys, you can add your public SSH key to GitHub and use the command given in the SSH tab. Copy the HTTPS command to your clipboard or temporary notepad and have it ready for your console or terminal. First, however, we’ll need to change into our source directory.

I make a folder called Source in my home directory, and I change into it with this on my Mac: 

cd ~/Source

This works on Linux, too. The tilde ( ~ ) is short for home directory. If you’re a Windows user, run this from your command prompt: 

cd %HOMEPATH%\Source

If you’re running Bash for Windows (i.e., Windows Subsystem for Linux), you can run the Linux commands in this section. The cd %HOMEPATH% command works only on the Windows command prompt or PowerShell prompt and not the Bash terminal.

Now that you’ve changed directory (i.e., cd ) into your Source directory, type git clone , press the spacebar, and then paste the command from the HTTPS tab of the Code pane in GitHub into the terminal, and run it. The completed command will look something like this: 

git clone https://github.com/clydebankmedia/JavaScript-CoffeeShopWebsite

When you fork a repository, a copy of it will be in your GitHub account. The command above represents the repository name in my account (note the rwoliver2 ). Your command will have the rwoliver2 substituted with your GitHub username, so be sure to use that copy instead of the exact link I have listed above.

If all has gone well, you now have JavaScript-CoffeeShopWebsite in ~/Source , so the full path should be ~/Source/JavaScript-CoffeeShopWebsite .

Now you can launch Visual Studio Code and open that folder to view and edit the code.

Committing Changes to Your Repository

If you make changes to the code and want to commit them to your fork, run this: 

git add filename.js

In this case, you’ll need to replace filename.js with the name of the file you want to add (e.g., main.js ). By adding the file, you are staging it to be committed. You can run this command on any number of files you wish (including entire directories), or you can run… 

git add .

…to add all the files (and files in folders) within this repository to be staged for commit. (Note the period, which means the current directory.) You can run… 

git status

…to see what changes are staged to be committed. If you run git status on a repository with no changes, you’ll see this: 

On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

nothing to commit, working tree clean

If you modify a file, then run git status , you’ll see something like this: 

On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Changes not staged for commit:
   (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
   (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
   modified:   main.js

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

In this case, we can see that main.js has been modified. This will include any file you have modified.

To commit this change to your local Git repository, you would first stage (add) the file (as above), then run the following: 

git commit -m "Short message describing your changes."

The message, specified by the -m argument (in this case, “Short message describing your changes.”) can be anything, but it’s helpful (to your future self and others) to provide detail about what you changed.

You can commit multiple files, or tell Git to commit all modified files (which skips the need to add them) via: 

git commit -a -m "A note about your changes."

The -a argument specifies “all,” meaning all changed files should be included in the commit.

Be careful when specifying the -a flag with git commit . You may include files that you aren’t quite ready to commit.

Pushing to Remote

The commit command commits changes to your local Git repository. However, if you want to sync them to GitHub, you’ll need to run this: 

git push origin main

The git push portion is the actual command, which tells Git we want to push our work to a remote repository. The origin portion tells Git where to push the changes. If we clone a repository from GitHub, the origin will be set to GitHub. The main portion indicates which branch to push.

Using Branches

Branches let you track separate sets of changes. For example, if you wanted to work on adding a particular feature, you could create a new branch for that. 

git checkout -b branch_name

This new branch (named whatever you put in the command above for branch_name ) will now receive any changes you commit. To push that branch, you’d run: 

git push origin branch_name

To switch branches, run… 

git checkout branch_name

…substituting the name of the branch you want to switch to in place of branch_name .

If you want to create (and change to) a new branch, use the -b argument, as previously described.

Branches are independent sets of changes (i.e., commits), so the changes you make in one branch won’t automatically carry over to others.

Viewing Changes

To view the changes, or the differences between your current set of files and the last commit, run… 

git diff

…which shows a “diff”, or difference summary, of the pending changes. You can press the Q key to exit the diff viewer.

Viewing Your Commit Log

As your Git repository grows with changes, you can use . . . 

git log

…to see a listing of all the commits you’ve made, which will look something like this: 

commit 6dd258b5273bc4a13eee201fd6304efc61baef5a (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD)
Author: Robert W. Oliver II <118407+rwoliver2@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Sun Jul 3 23:11:07 2022 -0500

   Update README.md

commit a2af786f19023bd2ac2d023ce8b2f2ed664f733b
Author: Robert W. Oliver II <118407+rwoliver2@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Sun Jul 3 23:07:07 2022 -0500

   Initial commit.

As with the diff command, press Q to exit the viewer. If there are few commits, the results will be displayed, and you’ll be returned to the command prompt.

You can also view a list of the commits that have been pushed to GitHub by going to the repository and clicking the “commits” icon (preceded by an icon and the number of commits) at the top of the file display.

Pull Requests

Now that you’ve committed changes to your repository and pushed them to your fork on GitHub, you can request that those changes be pulled into the official repository (in this case, https://github.com/clydebankmedia/JavaScript-CoffeeShopWebsite ) with a pull request.

To create a pull request, find your fork of the repository on GitHub. Click the Pull Requests tab at the top and then click the green New Pull Request button. In the “comparing changes” section, specify the repository and branch to pull from on the right and choose the destination on the left.

You’ll then be prompted to enter a message that describes the request. Submitting the request doesn’t automatically merge the changes. The maintainer of the official repository makes that decision, so including details in the message as to why they should accept the changes is helpful.

Syncing with the Official Repository

Over time, if other people are also merging changes into the official repository, it will become different from your fork of the repository. It’s a good idea to sync them as often as possible to prevent the two code bases from drifting far enough apart that a merge would require manual intervention.

To perform this sync, go to your fork of the repository in GitHub and click Fetch Upstream . If it says it’s behind, click Fetch and Merge . If all goes well, your repository will be automatically updated with changes from the official copy.

If you have altered your repository significantly, an automatic update may not be possible. In that case, you’ll have to complete further steps, which may include manually editing certain files. To prevent this, be sure to do regular syncs with the official repository.

Chapter Recap

» A Git repository is a collection of files and the changes to those files over time.

» It’s a good idea to fork a repository you plan to use, especially if you make changes to its code. You can also create a pull request, asking the maintainer of the official project to incorporate your changes.

» Branches are independent sets of changes to the files in a repository. You can switch branches at any time and commit changes to those individual branches. You can also sync those branches with the repository hosted on GitHub or any other Git hosting service via the push command.

Conclusion

Though your JavaScript career is just beginning, your effort throughout this book has given you a great deal of experience that will give you a tremendous advantage. Learning a new programming language—especially if you haven’t coded before—is no small achievement. You have a lot to be proud of!

We’ve covered the essentials, then toured JavaScript’s frontend and backend capabilities. We’ve also explored popular third-party libraries like jQuery and React. Not only have you learned the essentials of JavaScript, but you’ve also written code that you can use in your everyday projects.

Will you use your newfound knowledge to build a popular website? Perhaps you’re interested in creating a Node.js application to handle the requests for the next hot mobile game.

Whatever you choose, the options ahead for you are nearly limitless!

REMEMBER TO DOWNLOAD
YOUR FREE DIGITAL ASSETS!

Appendix I

HTML/CSS Quick Reference

This appendix is meant to serve as a refresher and quick reference for HTML and CSS. As such, it will read more as a reference and less as a guide. If you aren’t familiar with HTML/CSS, we recommend you check out HTML & CSS QuickStart Guide by David DuRocher, available at www.quickstartguides.com

Understanding HTML Structure

HyperText Markup Language (HTML) is a structured markup language. While you can use some HTML code outside of a full HTML document (e.g., web page), it’s important to understand the overall layout of an HTML file if you’re going to design a web page.

Elements and Tags

Before we get into the structure, let’s look at the basic building block of HTML: the element. Elements usually have an opening and closing tag, and content within them.

Let’s consider the paragraph element: 

<p>A paragraph of text would go here.</p>

The <p> portion is the opening tag, and the </p> portion is the closing tag. Between the two is the actual content that (usually) appears on the screen.

Elements have attributes. The attributes available vary, but id and class are perhaps the most important attributes. 

<p id="theId" class="theCssClass">
   Some text here.
</p>

The id attribute is used to give the element a referenceable value to be used in JavaScript and Cascading Style Sheets (CSS). The class attribute assigns CSS class names to an element.

Head

The <head> element is a special element with an open and closing tag ( <head> and </head> ) that contains special elements like <title> </title> and <meta> (meta has no closing tag) that define attributes about the web page for your browser and search engines. These elements aren’t visible to the user.

Body

The <body> element, which begins and ends with <body> and </body> , is where the bulk of the page lies, and makes up the visual portion of the page.

Comments

Any HTML code within comments is not shown on the page. 

<!-- This is an HTML comment. -->

HTML comments can span multiple lines. They start with <!-- and end with --> .

Using Divs and Semantic Elements

The most common element to use to group other elements together is <div> , which has an opening and closing tag: 

<div id="footer">
   <p>Copyright &copy; 2024 Your Company, All Rights Reserved.</p>
   <img src="images/logo.png" alt="Your Logo">
</div>

This is a very useful technique, but semantic elements provide a cleaner way to do this: 

<footer>
   <p>Copyright &copy; 2024 Your Company, All Rights Reserved.</p>
   <img src="images/logo.png" alt="Your Logo">
</footer>

Now you can apply styles via CSS directly to the footer element, rather than having to specify the id .

Here’s a list of semantic elements in HTML ( table 12 ):

Element

Purpose

<article>
</article>

Best used for an article, blog post, comment, or similar.

<aside></aside>

Great for call-outs, quotes, etc.

<details>
</details>

A toggle-like element that can show and hide additional details. Used with the <summary></summary> element.

<figcaption>
</figcaption>

Used to caption a figure.

<figure></figure>

Used to insert a figure into content. The <figcaption></figcaption> element can optionally be used inside the <figure></figure> element to caption the figure.

<footer>
</footer>

Typically used to display information at the bottom of the page.

<header>
</header>

Typically used to display information at the top of the page.

<main></main>

Helps group the dominant content portion of the <body></body> element. There should be only one <main></main> element on a page.

<mark></mark>

Highlights text within a larger collection of text (e.g., a <p></p> element).

<nav></nav>

Used to contain the navigation elements of the page (e.g., a menu or breadcrumb navigation).

<section>
</section>

A generic grouping of other elements. Should contain a heading (<h1></h1> , <h2></h2> , etc. element).

<summary>
</summary>

Within a < details></details> element, specifies the text that is clickable. The text outside the summary element, but within the details element, is hidden, displayed when the summary text is clicked.

<time></time>

Used to display a date/time value. The datetime attribute of this element allows for additional formatting.

I prefer to use semantic elements whenever possible. However, sometimes you need to use div elements when a semantic element to describe the grouping doesn’t exist or isn’t practical.

Frequently Used Elements

Here is a list of some of the most frequently used HTML elements ( table 13 ):

Element

Purpose

<h1></h1>

<h2></h2>

<h3></h3>

<h4></h4>

<h5></h5>

<h6></h6>

These heading elements allow for text within the tags to be displayed in larger, bolder fonts and serve as text structure of the page. H1 is the largest and H6 is the smallest.

<p></p>

A paragraph of text.

<a></a>

A link to another page. The text within the opening and closing tags is the text displayed for the link, and the href attribute (e.g., <a href=”page.html”> denotes the URL to navigate to.

<img>

The image element is used to display an image on the page. It does not have a closing tag.

<ul>

<li></li>

</ul>

An unordered list is a bullet list with <li></li> elements, each of which contains the text for one of the list items.

<ol>

<li></li>

</ol>

An ordered list (starting with 1, and incrementing with each item) with <li></li> elements, each of which contains the text for one of the list items. You can use the value I in the type attribute to display Roman numerals instead of numbers.

<div></div>

A generic but incredibly useful element to group other elements together.

<span></span>

Similar to <div></div> ; however, it is meant to work on smaller groups inline within divs.

<table>

<tr>

<td></td>

</tr>

</table>

Displays a table. Each <tr></tr> is a row, and each <td></td> is a cell.

Creating Forms

Forms allow you to provide a space on your web page to collect data from visitors: 

<form method="POST" action="url">
   <input type="email" name="email" value="">
   <input type="submit" name="submit" value="Submit">
</form>

In this example, the method attribute defines that the form will be sent via the HTTP verb POST, and the action attribute specifies the URL (in this case, I put “url” as a placeholder, but normally a real page or web address would go here).

Two input elements exist within this example. The first is the attribute type= " email " , which denotes a text input box which accepts and validates an email address. The name of the input box is also email . The second input element has type= " submit " , meaning it’s a submit button—the value of which sets the text to show on the button, in this case “Submit”.

Designing with Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)

HTML defines the structure and content of a document, while Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) applies style to the HTML elements in a cascading fashion (hence the name). By cascading, I mean that hierarchies of elements are considered when applying these styles.

A stylesheet is (usually) a separate file and has the extension of .css . You can include stylesheets in an HTML page within the <head></head> element like this: 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
   <head>
      <meta charset="UTF-8">
      <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
      <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="ie=edge">
      <title>An Example HTML Page</title>
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/style.css">
   </head>
   <body>
      <main>
         <p>Page content goes here!</p>
      </main>
   </body>
</html>

The line that adds the stylesheet in the above example is in bold type. Here it is separately… 

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/style.css">

This would include a file called style.css in the css folder.

CSS files contain rules like this: 

body {
   font-family: "Open Sans";
}

.boldText { font-weight: bold; }

Rules contain selectors, which, in the example above, would be body and .boldText . The body selector will apply the rule within the curly braces (in this case, setting the font to Open Sans) to all HTML elements within the body (hence the cascading part of the acronym CSS).

The second rule shown is a CSS class, which can be applied with the class attribute on any HTML element. So, if these two CSS rules were active in our file, we can apply the class .boldText to a span within a paragraph to bold that particular portion. 

<p>Learning JavaScript is <span class="boldText">FUN</span>!</p>

You can apply a rule to any HTML element, custom class, or a particular ID (defined by the id attribute on an HTML element).

CSS File 

#specialPart { font-weight: bold; }

HTML File 

<div id="specialPart">
   <p>Something really special!</p>
</div>

CSS classes can be applied to multiple HTML elements, and each HTML element class attribute can contain multiple CSS classes, separated by a space. But IDs belong to only one element on the page. An element may have both an ID and a class.

Comments can be inserted into CSS files like this: 

/* This line will not be processed as a CSS rule */

The Box Model

The box model is a paradigm in web development that envisions rectangular boxes around HTML elements. The box in the center contains the element’s content. This content is sized via the width and height CSS properties. But the element consumes more space than the content’s width and height. It is surrounded by a layer called padding, or the padding box.

The next layer outward is the border. In many cases, this isn’t defined, but you can set a border around an element and whatever size the border is becomes the additional space taken up by the main element. It’s important to note that the padding lies between the border and the element, so if you add padding, the border will appear to be separate from the element. Finally, the margin box is the amount of space between the element in question and other elements.

If a rectangular element has a width of 100 pixels and a height of 50 pixels, and a padding, border, and margin all set to 1 pixel for all sides, then the actual space the element will consume on the page will be at least 106 pixels of width and 56 pixels tall. To calculate this, consider that the width of an element includes the padding, border, and margin values of both left and right sides. Likewise, the height of an element includes the padding, border, and margin values of the top and bottom sides ( figure 39 ).

The margins aren’t technically considered part of the element, but rather part of the space around it.

Colors

You can specify colors in CSS in several ways. The simplest is to use one of the CSS color names that are supported in all browsers. There are 140 colors in the collection—too many to list here (see https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/named-color for a full list). Let’s work with some examples: 

.redText { color: red; }
.blueText { color: blue; }
.orangeText { color: orange; }

You can also specify colors in hexadecimal format: 

.redText { color: #FF0000; }

Hexadecimal colors use hex values for red, green, and blue. You’ll note that FF is in the first spot, meaning FF (256 in decimal) units of red, 00 (0 in decimal) units of green, and 00 (0 in decimal) units in blue. This will yield a very bright red.

There are many tools on the web (and in web design programs) that can give you hex colors via a color picker. Here’s one I use quite often: https://htmlcheatsheet.com . It’s also worth noting that Visual Studio Code puts a little character-sized square of the color inline as a handy reference as you type.

If the color I want to use is in the list of 140 browser-supported color names, I use it, if possible. This works well and is easy to remember. I’d rather memorize lemonchiffon than #FFFACD, or royalblue instead of #4169E1.

Fonts

You can specify fonts in CSS, as we did in a previous example: 

body {
   font-family: "Open Sans";
}

There are quite a few fonts that are available in most browsers and systems, like Arial, Helvetica, Verdana, etc., and generic names like sans-serif, serif, cursive, and monospace.

Google Fonts gives you a wide assortment of very nice-looking fonts and even gives you the code to use. Visit https://fonts.google.com/ to browse the fonts, click one, then select your desired weight (400 is considered regular), then click the plus icon to view the <link> tag to import the font.

In the years I’ve been using Google Fonts, the interface has changed quite a few times, so things might look different for you than I described. However, the general paradigm of picking your font, selecting the weight (or style, like italic), then clicking a button to see the CSS code, has remained.

Responsive Design

The topic of responsive design—that is, web design that looks good on all devices, from computers, through tablets, to smart phones—could fill its own book. This topic is covered in depth in HTML & CSS QuickStart Guide by David DuRocher. To summarize the concept here, you can specify media queries within your CSS file to tailor CSS rules to particular device sizes.

Here’s a simple example: 

/* This part applies to the entire file */

   body {
      font-family: "Open Sans";
   }

      .redText { color: red; }

   #logo {
      width: 100px;
      height: 80px;

   /* This part applies to devices with a maximum width of 500 pixels */
   @media screen and (max-width: 500px) {
      #logo {
         width: 50px;
         height: 40px;
      }
   }

In this CSS example, the HTML element with the ID of logo will have a width of 100 pixels and a height of 80 pixels, unless you’re on a device with a maximum width of 500 pixels (like a small cell phone). In that case, the CSS rule(s) within the curly braces will apply. Here, that would make the width of the logo 50 pixels and the height 40 pixels.

Appendix II

Using the http-server Node.js Package

As we’ve discussed throughout the book, you can browse HTML files with Google Chrome locally—that is, directly—by loading them in the web browser. This works fine for most cases, but some features, like cookies, don’t work in this mode.

To test cookies, your web pages need to be hosted on a web server. A simple solution for this is to install the http-server Node.js package. Fortunately, this process is easy no matter which operating system you’re running.

Simply launch your terminal (or command prompt) and run the command: 

npm install --global http-server

Once this is done, the http-server command is available. To use, change to any directory in the terminal with the cd command, like this…

Windows 

cd %USERPROFILE%\Source\coffee-shop

macOS and Linux 

cd ~/Source/coffee-shop

…then run the http-server command, like this… 

http-server

You can also specify the path at the end of the http-server command and omit the cd step. This is helpful if you want to put this command in a script or batch file. To do this, run…

Windows 

http-server %USERPROFILE%\Source\coffee-shop

macOS and Linux 

http-server ~/Source/coffee-shop

In either example, change Source/coffee-shop to the path of your source code folder with the index.html file you wish to view.

If all goes well, you should see something like this in the terminal window: 

Starting up http-server, serving ./

http-server version: 14.1.1

http-server settings:
CORS: disabled
Cache: 3600 seconds
Connection Timeout: 120 seconds
Directory Listings: visible
AutoIndex: visible
Serve GZIP Files: false
Serve Brotli Files: false
Default File Extension: none

Available on:
   http://127.0.0.1:8080
   http://10.0.0.63:8080
Hit CTRL-C to stop the server

If http-server doesn’t start (i.e., you get a command not found or similar error message), try closing the terminal and restarting it.

Now you can copy one of the links displayed in the “Available on:” section (I recommend choosing the 127.0.0.1 link) and paste this into your browser. Going to http://127.0.0.1:8080/ will show you the index.html and other pages upon request from the current directory.

If you’re using this to test the coffee shop, you can now open the JavaScript console and watch as you add items to the cart. You can run getCart() in the console to see the cart stored in the cookies.

Appendix III

Using Common Third-Party Libraries

Sometimes we all need a little help from our friends. With JavaScript, our friends include some helpful third-party libraries that smooth over the rough edges in JavaScript. Here are some of my favorites, along with quick overviews of how to use them.

currency.js

Formatting currency and working with floating-point numbers can be tricky in JavaScript, but fortunately, the currency.js library can help. The currency.js library is extremely lightweight and simple to use.

Installation

There are multiple ways to install currency.js , but the simplest is to download the JavaScript source file to your local website files and include it via a <script> tag. You can visit https://currency.js.org to obtain the link. As of publication, the Download currency.js button at the top of the page is a direct link to the JavaScript source of the library. You can save this to your source code folder by clicking the three-dot menu in Chrome and selecting Save and share then Save page as…

You can also use npm to download the file to your project automatically if you’d like. However, the instructions here will focus on simply including the downloaded file in your project.

Assuming you save the currency.js file to your source code folder, and the HTML file that uses it is in the same folder, the HTML file would look like this:

currency.html 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
   <head>
      <meta charset="UTF-8">
      <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
      <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="ie=edge">
      <title>Using currency.js</title>
   </head>
   <body>
      <script src="currency.min.js"></script>
   </body>
</html>

Usage

The principal workflow of currency.js involves creating currency objects with the values you need. These objects contain the value and the necessary methods and internal logic to properly handle currency and floating-point numbers.

To run this code, either place the code samples below in a <script></script> tag on the currency.html page or load the page in the browser and use the JavaScript console.

The filename you download from the official website is named currency.min.js, a minified version of the currency.js script. This is why we load it with <script src=”currency.min.js”></script> . The min in the filename isn’t what makes it minified, as any .js file can be minified, but this generally is an indication it is minified. In any case, you’ll have to make sure the filename in the src attribute of the script tag matches the actual filename.

For example, if we wanted to create a currency object with a price, it would look something like this: 

let price = currency(4.95)

We can now discount this price without fear of any floating-point variable issues: 

// Price with 20% discount
let discountedPrice = price.multiply(0.8)

To display the discountedPrice variable, we can now use… 

console.log(discountedPrice.format())

…which displays… 

$3.96

If you want to display the currency symbol for your locale, you can assign it when you create the currency object: 

// Use Euro currency
let price = currency(4.95, { symbol: "€" })

Using methods like add , subtract , multiply , and divide on the resulting currency object allows for correct mathematical calculations.

You can even chain calculations together in a single function: 

// Start with 4.95
let price = currency(4.95)

// Add 2.25 to the price then subtract 3.16
let newPrice = price.add(2.25).subtract(3.16)

// Display the new price
console.log(newPrice.format())

For more information about the capabilities of currency.js , visit currency.js.org .

Moment.js

The moment.js JavaScript library makes it easy to work with time, dates, and time zones.

Installation

As with currency.js , there are several ways to install moment.js . However, to keep things simple, we’ll download the JavaScript source file and include it via a script tag. You can download the file from https://momentjs.com . As of publication, there are four files you can download, but essentially two versions—one with locales and one without. If you don’t need support for internationalization features (sometimes abbreviated as i18n in programming), I’d recommend downloading the moment.js version.

When I said there were four files, both the locale and non-locale versions have a regular and minified version. For local use, I’d recommend the regular version ( moment.js and moment-with-locales.js ). However, for website use, it’s preferable to use the minified version (with the min.js extension) to reduce download time.

Assuming you save the moment.js file to your source code folder, and the HTML file that uses it is in the same folder, the HTML file would look like this:

moment.html 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
   <head>
      <meta charset="UTF-8">
      <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
      <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="ie=edge">
      <title>Using moment.js</title>
   </head>
   <body>
      <script src="moment.js"></script>
   </body>
</html>

The non-minified version of moment.js is easily readable in the browser, or in Visual Studio Code. Browsing other people’s code can be very informative, and you’ll probably learn some new techniques, so I’d recommend checking it out.

Usage

To run this code, either place the code samples below in a <script></script> tag on the moment.html page or load the page in the browser and use the JavaScript console.

First, let’s get the current time and date with moment, but in a format of our choosing. 

// Set the now variable to the current time and date
let now = moment().format("MMMM Do, YYYY @ h:mm:ss a")

// Display it
console.log(now)

When I run this code in my JavaScript console (with moment.html loaded), I see: 

September 30th, 2024 @ 6:17:11pm

This is the current time at which I’m writing this appendix. Yours will be different, of course. And, if you like, you can format it a bit differently than I did. You can remove the @ symbol between the time and date, or remove the commas. But if you’d like to change the formatting codes (e.g., MMMM , Do , h:mm:ss , etc.), you can refer to the formatting codes at the momentjs.com/ website, which, as of publication, are found at momentjs.com/docs/#/displaying/format.

But moment.js does far more than simply format dates. One of my favorite features is relative time. Adding minutes, hours, or dates to dates can be annoying, but moment.js makes it easy: 

// Set the now variable to the current time and date
let now = moment()

// Add 1 hour, then display it
let inOneHour = now.add(1, "hours")
console.log(inOneHour.format("MMMM Do, YYYY @ h:mm:ss a"))

In this example, I don’t add the format method until I’m ready to use it. By default, setting a variable to the result of moment() returns the current time and date. I can perform any calculations to that time I want without being concerned about formatting until I am ready to display it on a page (or, in this case, the JavaScript console).

We can also find out the difference between two dates: 

// Obtain the current time
let now = moment()

// Obtain a time in the past
let past = moment("2000-01-01")

// Display the difference between the two times
console.log('The start of the new millennium was about ${past.from(now)}.')

When I run this code, I see: 

The start of the new millennium was about 25 years ago.

I feel old reading that sentence!

To learn more about moment.js and its features, including locale and time zone support, which we don’t have space to cover here, go to momentjs.com .

Glossary

AJAX

Asynchronous JavaScript and XML is a technology that lets JavaScript make requests to a backend server, typically exchanging JSON with the service.

Anonymous function

A function that has no name.

Application programming interface (API)

A way for two or more computer programs to communicate with each other. It’s a way for our code to interact with a particular service or functionality.

Argument

A value that can be passed to a function.

Array

A type of variable that contains multiple values.

Asynchronous

A program execution method that allows for multiple bits of code to run at once and usually without blocking the operation of other parts of the code. These bits of code can start, run, and finish in time periods that overlap one another.

Backend

Code that usually runs on a server that can store data and perform business logic. This portion usually delivers results to the frontend.

Beautification

The process of formatting source code in a way that is pleasing to the eye and easy to browse.

Boolean

A value that is either true or false and needs no further evaluation.

Branching

The process of copying code to a new, separate version in a software project.

Bug

An error or unexpected behavior in software.

Camel case

The style of writing variable names that involves a mix between lower case and upper-case letters, resembling the humps on a camel. The first word in the variable name isn’t capitalized, but the first letter of subsequent words is capitalized: for example, firstName . If the variable name is a single word, it is left all lowercase.

Capturing group

A feature of regular expressions that enables the capture of part of the match text with parentheses, facilitating later reuse, if needed.

Case insensitive

An attribute of a search where the case of the result is not important and considered a match if the letter(s) are the same.

Class

A template for organizing data and logic.

Clone

The process of downloading a copy of a Git repository to your computer.

Closure

A technique of scoping variables and keeping those scopes active, even after the containing scope has finished.

Code editor

A text editor that has special features that make it easier to write code.

Comparison

A decision, based on the difference(s) between two or more values, that can affect the flow of a program.

Concatenation

The process of joining strings together.

Content delivery network (CDN)

A globally distributed network that accelerates web page delivery by caching assets as close to the visitor as possible.

Cookie

A small fragment of data from a website that is stored within a web browser and that the website can retrieve later.

CORS

Short for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, a protocol that governs the permissions for a web page to make requests to another domain.

Design pattern

The methodology used to lay out the data and logic in a program.

Evaluating

The process of computing the value of an expression, which can involve variables, logical comparisons, arithmetic operations, or function calls. This is akin to solving or simplifying an equation in mathematics.

Float

A real number containing a decimal point.

Fork

In relation to Git repositories, the process of copying a repository to make changes without interfering with the original copy.

Form

A collection of input elements on a web page that collects data from the user and can transfer that data to a backend process via GET or POST.

Frontend

The user interface or code that runs in the web browser for user interaction. Typically involves HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Full-stack

Refers to both the frontend and backend of a site, including everything from the HTML and CSS to the server code that processes requests.

Function

A block of code that performs a specific task. Functions can be called by other code and can accept arguments and return values.

Function expression

A variable that is set to a function. Function expressions enable you to create a function and then assign that function to a variable, rather than naming the function outright.

GET request

A type of web request that only reads data from a web server.

Global event

An event that occurs within the document rather than from some interaction the user has with an HTML element.

Header

A part of an HTTP request or response sent before the body content that sets configuration and metadata to the client about a request.

Hoisted

In JavaScript, a variable or function that is available before it is defined within the same scope.

HTML event

An event that occurs because of a user interaction with a web page.

Immutable

Read-only, unchangeable.

Index

In reference to arrays, the position of a particular value in the array.

Infinite loop

A loop that continues to execute without a reachable condition to break.

Instantiation

The act of creating an object, usually from a class, but in JavaScript this can also be done by prototyping the object in code without a class.

Integer

A whole number, either negative or positive (or zero).

IP address

The unique numerical address of a computer (or network interface) on a network.

Iteration

A single cycle through a block of code, usually as part of a loop.

JSON

JavaScript Object Notation, a format useful for data exchange, both within JSON and with other programming languages. It is widely supported and has a human-readable syntax.

Lexical scope

Describes how functions in JavaScript have access to variables based on where those variables are defined within the code.

Localization

The process of adjusting a program to enable input from and produce output in various locales using international standards for time, currency, and language.

Logical comparison

A type of comparison that uses a logical operator, such as AND, OR, or NOT. This can be used to compare the result between multiple comparative operations.

Merging

The process of bringing different branched versions in source code or a Git repository back together, integrating the changes into a unified copy.

Metadata

In the context of web pages, data provided in the header that provides information about the page to search engines and web browsers.

Method

A function that is part of an object or class.

Minification

In the context of JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, the result of code that has been stripped of unnecessary spaces, newline characters, and comments. This is usually done for speed and efficiency. The result is sometimes referred to as “minified” and the process to “minify” a file.

Nested function

A function that contains other functions.

Network protocol

An established method of exchanging data over a network.

Object

A collection of associated data and logic.

Object-oriented programming

A paradigm in programming that uses objects and classes to organize and bundle data and logic.

Operator

A character, or group of characters, that performs an operation (e.g., arithmetic, comparison, etc.).

Parameterized

The process of allowing values to be passed to a function, thereby adding flexibility.

Port

A numerical identifier to distinguish between multiple services listening or connecting to other services over a network.

POST request

A type of web request that sends data to a web server.

Promise

An object containing code that can take a long time to run. This code is commonly referred to as the producing code. The consuming code, which relies on the results of the producing code, is “promised” a value or an error.

Property

A variable attached to an object.

Prototypal inheritance

A technique that provides a way to give objects the ability to acquire methods and properties from other objects.

Pull request

A request to the maintainer(s) of a software project for permission to merge changes into the main project.

Regular expression

A set of symbols with the power to search through strings and match, or change, specific portions of those strings.

Render

The process of displaying content to a user.

Repository

A container that stores source code.

Scope

A way to describe and determine what parts of the code can access and modify a variable.

Singleton

A design pattern that restricts a class to instantiate only a single object.

Single-page application

A web application that updates content on a single page, providing an interactive experience without requiring a full page reload.

Source code management

The process of tracking changes in code and synchronizing them for purposes of collaboration.

State

The status of a program’s execution, including the execution position and all the variables and data structures within it.

String

A variable that contains characters and text.

Synchronous

A program execution method that requires code to run in sequence, one after another.

Syntactic sugar

Syntax in a programming language that makes features easier to write without changing the underlying functionality.

Syntax

The rules and structure of code in programming languages.

Template literals or template strings

A feature introduced in ES6 that allows embedding expressions inside of a string and multiline strings.

Thread

A separate path of execution through a program that can start, run, and finish at different (and possibly overlapping) times.

Undeclared variable

A variable that does not have a declared scope. An undeclared variable becomes global by default, which can create errors due to the lack of specific scope within your code.

Variable

A container for values like strings, numbers, and objects.

Viewport

The portion of the browser’s window that is usable for HTML content, minus any scrollbars or similar browser features.

Whitespace

Usually a space character, but broadly defined as characters (or a group of characters) that serve as a separation between other characters or words.
